title: The Meaning of Non-Existence and the Patient Psalmist
english: unspoken and glorified. 'Do not disregard me, for I am a sojourner in this land.' Do not disregard me while I am praying, entreating, weeping, and bearing tears—such things as 'those who sow in joy shall reap.' Therefore, 'do not disregard me,' but having responded, give what I have requested; for disregard sometimes signifies delay and patience, and sometimes indeed patience, when it occurs regarding sins: 'having done these things, I was silent' (Psalm 39:8), instead of 'I have not repaid you.' If I were an inhabitant, I would not have dared to ask and to pray. For the inhabitants are those responsible for wickedness and impiety. For it is said in Jeremiah: 'from the face of the north shall the evils be burned upon those inhabiting the land' (Jeremiah 50:39), not 'upon those sojourning.' And in the Revelation of John, it is said three times: 'woe, woe, woe upon those inhabiting the land' (Revelation 18:7). If I were, therefore, an inhabitant, I would not have said, 'do not disregard me.'

And I am a stranger just as all my fathers were. The sojourner and the stranger are one and the same. For Paul, having made a list of all those who were well-pleasing through faith in the Epistle to the Hebrews, called them sojourners and strangers (Hebrews 11:13). None of them is an inhabitant, none is a native, but a stranger. He has come from elsewhere into this place; he was not born here. Therefore, all the fathers according to virtue were sojourners in the land and strangers, such as the patriarchs and others who produced according to divine instruction, such as prophets, teachers, and lawgivers.

Refresh me, so that I may find refreshment before I depart and no longer exist. Here, refreshment is called praiseworthy, being equivalent to 'delighting in the Lord.' 'I found refreshment for myself,' says Ephrem. And that refreshment is a slight thing. One refreshes praiseworthily when he enjoys virtue, when he 'delights in the Lord,' when he perceives and receives the understanding of the 'paradise of delight.' Since, therefore, much is lacking to me—for this is why I send up a petition, so that I may be filled of the things lacking—for this also he said at the beginning of the Psalm: 'Lord, make known to me my end and the number of my days, what it is, so that I may know what I lack' (Psalm 39:4). When he knows the things that are lacking and acquires these, he finds refreshment through such possessions. Therefore, he says: refresh me to remain in this life, so that having been instructed, I may [be refreshed]...

I shall refresh myself before I depart from this life and no longer exist. He does not say, 'I shall not begin to be,' but rather, 'I shall be such a person as I desire to be'; for the soul does not move into non-existence. Listen, accordingly, to what is said to people: one must take the words in their proper sense. If the righteous man or the wise man says according to God, 'I strive for all things so that I may become rich' (cf. Prov 28:20), do not take what is said to mean material wealth. But if someone else were a rhetorician or a physician—and this one is therefore a holy wise man—he says, 'I have no other endurance except the Lord and the subsistence from Him.'

Thus, if this wise man says, 'Let me live most hopefully in this only life, so that I may refresh myself having eaten and drunk according to: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Luke 12:19), one must take the refreshment appropriately to the person, both the 'let me' and the 'no longer to be.' He who says this is immortal. Therefore, if he says, 'I shall no longer be,' he does not say, 'I move into complete destruction, I turn into non-existence,' but rather, 'I shall no longer be in the way that I desired to have been.' If a sinner says, 'Admonish me, discipline me, so that I may no longer be'—for it is not so that he may move into complete destruction.

1–2 unto the end; the Psalm of David: 'Waiting, I waited upon the Lord, and He attended to me' (Ps 40:1). The preceding Psalm could have been spoken by any saint who has lived his life with patience and magnanimity, and by the Lord's man; for the Apostle, taking words from it, has set forth in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning Christ those things having been said. This is the whole: 'A sacrifice and an offering You did not desire' (Heb 10:5), until: 'It is written about me in the head of a book' (Ps 40:7). And the Psalm is single-personed. The same person who began announces and sings until the end of the Psalm. He therefore says thankfully to God: 'Waiting, I waited upon the Lord, and He heard my prayer.' The 'waiting, I waited' has such a meaning as if someone were to say, 'I healed medically, I wrote grammatically.' They are waiting, not in a manner of mere waiting, but either through much insensitivity or sometimes through ambition. For the Apostle says: 'I will not deliver my body so that I may boast' (1 Cor 9:27), because of praise.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Soul's Descent and Christ's Identification with Human Misery
english: He does not merely say 'having endured, I remained' as if to please the body and soul; rather, he endured with knowledge and as was necessary, not to receive a prize, glory, or praise from men. To endure thus is to say, as I might say, 'I acted wisely according to wisdom.' It was said in the preceding psalm that God is the endurance of the righteous: 'And now, what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 70:5). He who bears the heavy things falling upon him through this endurance says, 'Having endured, I remained with the Lord.' He bore the heavy things with an enduring disposition, for many, as I have said, bear the heavy things for some [other] reason. God is therefore the endurance of the holy. And in Jeremiah it is indeed said: 'A throne of glory rising, our holiness, endurance of Israel, Lord of Israel' (Jeremiah 33:16). He who is therefore established according to this endurance and is named from it says, 'Having endured, I remained with the Lord,' speaking as a slave. He who serves God calls him 'Lord' through his deeds, his mindsets, and his words. This one says, 'In the Holy Spirit, Lord Jesus'; for not everyone who calls Jesus Lord does so in this Spirit, but hypocrites indeed do this. Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord' (Matthew 7:21-23), and what does he say to them? 'I never knew you.' I never knew you having served me. And again: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Matthew 7:23). Therefore, he who calls Jesus thus Lord, doing the will of his Father in heaven, is the one who calls him 'in the Holy Spirit' Lord. The voice is therefore that of a slave.

And he heard my prayer. Being in distress, I cried out, and God, attending to my prayer, has fulfilled these things. For I 'having endured, I remained' [obeyed] the commandment concerning which the Savior said, 'He who endures to the end, this one will be saved' (Matthew 24:13). The 'I remained' is a state of having come to rest. And what kind of face did the Lord have? For we have not spoken out of necessity. If, then, you take it from the face of the Savior—for it has become a matter of pre-passion, it has not become a matter of passions—Jesus 'began to be amazed and distressed' (Mark 14:33). Such things happened to him until the beginning. We do not say that pre-passion occurs without disturbance; for we do not say that anyone other than the Trinity is without disturbance.

For the soul, which Jesus took up, is something other than the Trinity; it is of a nature to receive passion and the beginning of being terrified and distressed. And I say according to the apostles: 'Instead of the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising shame' (Heb 12:2). If it had not become a victor in passion, it would not have been a feat or a contest.

Furthermore: the 'pay attention to me' [is] instead of 'he sighed'. And he brought me up out of the pit of misery and from the clay of matter. If each of the saints says this, 'the pit of misery' refers to the place concerning the earth; for a pit is a place where the waters falling from above gather. Often, in the divine writings, both the place concerning the earth and Hades are signified by this name; for when in the twenty-ninth [Psalm] it is said according to the man: 'You have saved me from those going down into the pit' (Ps 29:15), I do not myself go down into a pit. Because of others, I have been there. No one else brought me down.

Moreover, this appears more clearly from: 'I was counted among those going down into the pit; I became as a helpless man among the dead, yet free' (Ps 29:15). I am not one of those being led into the pit, but I 'was counted'. I counted myself among those. Therefore, I 'became' 'as a helpless man'. Not being helpless, he became as helpless; for when the Jews came to seize him, if he had not delivered himself, they would not have been able to take him. If he is 'free among the dead', he is not one of those becoming [members] of Hades by nature through choice and action, but he counted himself into this.

Therefore, he 'brought me up' 'from the pit of misery'. He who humbled his own body and enslaved it, and while still walking upon the earth, having acquired his citizenship in the heavens, he was lifted up from the pit of misery and from the clay of matter. And now indeed he was lifted up in power from the world and from matter and from the clay, from which the clay body has sailed. 'And God formed man from dust from the earth' (Gen 2:7). And even Job says: 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:9). And Jesus will also say this according to the man: I have become into the pit of misery, I was counted, so that I might free them from misery and from the clay of matter; for because of them, I have become into the clay of matter.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The New Song and the Hope of the Lord
english: When this corruptible body is changed into incorruption, it is no longer held by the surrounding mud and distress, but has been rescued from these things. 'And he set my feet upon a rock.' Let this be said generally concerning the righteous. Regarding 'rock,' let the unbroken and indivisible Word of God be heard in these matters, which no storm or tempest moves. Often, indeed, the memory of a rock becomes a memorial of the holy words, not capable of being grasped by sensation; for when the saint says thankfully to God, 'Lift me up on a rock,' he does not say, 'He placed me suspended on a sensible rock,' but upon the unbroken and indivisible Word.

Paul interpreted this rock and said who it is, that it is Christ: 'for they drank from a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). And again this same hymnographer says with other things: 'their strong ones laid down the rock they were carrying.' Those of the Egyptians, approaching the rock, were seen as nothing. And just as 'Aaron's rod overcame the rods' (Exod 7:12) of the Egyptians who were singing, that is, he conquered them. When therefore it is said, 'Death is swallowed up' (1 Cor 15:54), 'Israel is swallowed up.' When those who think themselves strong—sophists, certain contentious men, or even evil spirits—approach the rock, they are swallowed up, proving themselves to be nothing.

Upon this rock, Christ, whom the approaching strong ones of the Egyptians are swallowed up by, the feet of the one being benefited stand, to be saved from shaking and tempest and having enemies. Endurance is produced. He does not always suffer these things when he is in the pit of distress, when he is in the mud of matter; endurance is produced. But he does not always suffer these things. When he comes out of these, the end of endurance having been received, the feet of the one having been benefited stand, therefore, upon the said rock. 'And he directed my steps' (Ps 119:133). And see how the Word leads us far into the history. No one standing walks, no one walking stands. When someone is therefore made firm according to Christ so as to be able to say, 'Who shall separate us from the love of God?' (Rom 8:35), his steps have directed paths; for he always hastens toward the higher things, toward the heavenly, being directed by God.

The steps of the runner: for it is 'not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy' (Ps 107:13). And he cast into my mouth a new song (Ps 40:9). 'Into the mouth' of the inner man, that is, into my word. 'A new song': often for us... regarding the new, how it is said. That which is uninterrupted is always new, while that which has been succeeded is old. And through many examples it has often been demonstrated.

A hymn to our God. He who was lifted up from the aforementioned circumstances of the pit of misery and the mire of matter obtained an uninterrupted victory. The victory of the uninterrupted is a new triumph. What is this new song? It explains: it is a 'hymn' 'to our God.' When we hymn God, when we receive His praise, as far as possible, becoming in perfection, we sing a new song; for that which is in perfection is uninterrupted. Therefore also the hymn which is sent up to God thankfully within it is a new song.

Many shall see and shall be afraid and shall hope in the Lord (Ps 37:7). 'Many shall see,' having seen me lifted up from the pit of misery and from the mire of matter, and having my feet established upon the rock, and my steps being directed, and me singing and hymning; 'and they shall be afraid' so that they too might come into such a guidance, 'and they shall hope' so that they too might attain these things which already exist for me.

Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord (Ps 37:7). David once had a single combat against Goliath and did not hope in a shield. You see that the name of the Lord has become his hope. And it is said regarding the Lord being signified by hope—and there is no other hope than the expectation of good things—that often some say of things already existing, 'my hope.' The wealthy indeed say 'my hope,' not regarding what is expected, but what is already present. And therefore, those who already possess the name of the Lord consider it to be hope.

And he did not look toward vanities and false delusions. He who looks toward the Lord does not look toward vanities and false delusions. He does not look toward wealth, nor toward greatness of body, nor toward military might, nor toward any other of those things which are able to fail. And 'delusions' are called 'false,' the divinations. They are...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
